column3: It nearly repeats the focus: clear recited signs are called manifest magic when truth arrives.
It identifies the Quran as a clear book, supplying the positive quality that the focus's opponents resist.
It condemns fabricating a lie about God but does not depict the reception of revealed signs.
Musa's clear signs are called fabricated magic and rejected as unknown to the ancestors.
It concerns jinn learning that they do not know the unseen after Sulayman's death.
It reverses the focus's fabrication charge by identifying deniers of God's signs as the liars.
Clear recited signs meet an evasive demand to bring back the ancestors rather than an answer to the signs.
The preceding local ayah gives the punishment for those who denied it, framing the focus's accusation.
The nearby accusation that the messenger fabricated a lie supplies the immediate setting for the focus.
Deniers answer clear recited signs by treating social status and gathering as proof.
It describes the truth of death's intoxication, not reception of revelation.
Nuh's people find his standing and reminder through God's signs burdensome, showing resistance to warning.
Deniers call the Quran a fabricated falsehood made with human help, directly matching the focus's label.
It supplies the local backdrop that this audience had received neither earlier scripture nor a warner.
It gives the recurring bare accusation that the message is manifest magic.
Opponents ask for the clear recitation to be replaced, while the messenger grounds it in revelation rather than invention.
It warns against being turned away from God's verses after their descent, the pressure alleged in the focus.
It affirms a wise recitation of signs but does not develop opposition or ancestral worship.
Deniers reduce recited signs to ancient tales and claim they could produce the like.
It places the local denial among earlier peoples' denial of messengers and its consequence.
It calls the false gods and claims of a ruined people their fabrication, without a revelation-reception scene.
Elite deniers call a human messenger self-seeking and invoke what their forefathers never heard.
It states that arriving truth guides or misguides to each person's own account, clarifying the response at issue.
It names the active obstruction of believers from God's path and its portrayal as crooked.
Deniers dismiss guidance because believers reached it first, then call it an old fabrication.
It states that clear signs are sent down and that God guides whom He wills.
It declares that God does what He wills without clarifying the focus relation.
A warning messenger from among them provokes astonishment, then accusations of magic and lying.
Truth from God is immediately relabeled manifest magic, closely matching the focus's final charge.
It concerns gossip about the ruler's wife and Yusuf.
Visible signs are directly recast as manifest magic despite their illuminating character.
Musa challenges the reflex of calling truth magic and distinguishes it from magic's failure.
Even a tangible written book would be relabeled manifest magic by the deniers.
The warning and good news revealed to a human messenger are met by the accusation of manifest magic.
It records Pharaoh summoning skilled magicians, not a judgment of revelation.
It describes punishment in Hell without a relation to the focus's reception scene.
It calls a circulating slander manifest falsehood, only a distant parallel to the fabrication label.
It begins Musa's encounter with the magicians without the relevant accusation or response.
It questions the desire for false gods, broadly related to the inherited worship contested in the focus.
Messengers are accused of trying to turn people from ancestral worship and are asked for clear authority.
It answers rejection with the challenge to produce a more guiding book from God.
It condemns every sinful habitual fabricator without locating the charge in a revelation scene.
Salih's people resist leaving their fathers' worship and express troubling doubt about his call.
Failure to answer revealed guidance is identified as following desire without divine guidance.
It prohibits women from bringing fabricated slander, a different use of fabrication.
Hud's people explicitly object that his call requires abandoning what their fathers worshipped.
On the Day of judgment, demanded proof makes their fabrications vanish and truth belong to God.
The fabrication accusation is answered by a public challenge to produce comparable fabricated surahs.
Clear proofs brought by the awaited messenger are labeled manifest magic.
It characterizes the God-fearing by unseen fear and concern for the Hour.
A people reject their messenger by calling him a man who fabricated a lie about God.
It identifies their worship as the unexamined continuation of their fathers' worship.
It gives the bare ancestral rationale for idol worship: their fathers were worshippers of them.
It tersely describes being turned away from the truth without the focus's social or revelatory scene.
Shuayb's opponents explicitly resent leaving ancestral worship and losing unrestricted control of wealth.
It declares the arrival of truth and the passing of falsehood, the positive reversal of the focus's labels.
Hypocrites use oaths as cover and thereby turn others from God's path.
The local deniers mock the messenger's report of resurrection, but not the clear signs of the focus.
It describes every soul arriving with a driver and witness.
When God's verses are recited, the denier calls them ancient tales.
It shows the nearby status-based objection that revelation should have gone to a great man of the two towns.
It states that every destroyed town had a known decree.
It condemns inventing divine legal labels, not the rejection of a received recitation.
It rejects the claim that God reveals nothing to a human and recalls the guiding book given to Musa.
It directly joins fabricating a lie about God with denying His signs.
It introduces the true recitation of Musa and Pharaoh's story for believers.
It regulates marriage to women previously married to one's fathers.
It depicts the final loss of fabricated claims when every soul is returned to God.
It gives the punishment for those who persistently reject God's signs.
Deniers recast their human messenger as a man possessed and defer judgment on him.
Musa warns the magicians not to fabricate a lie about God.
It affirms that God's verses are recited in truth and that God does not will injustice.
It describes Satan turning people from remembrance and prayer through wine and gambling.
It records the magicians' private dispute and secret counsel.
The condemned are reminded that God's verses were recited to them and they denied them.
It contrasts the claim that the messenger is possessed with the truth he brought, which most hate.
Arriving truth is rejected through demands for Musa's signs and the claim that the two messages are supporting magic.
Salih is dismissed as one bewitched, a related way of discrediting a messenger rather than his evidence.
Satan says he only invited people and they answered, an indirect account of misleading influence.
It records the condemned admitting that their misery overcame them and they strayed.
It repeats the pairing of fabrication about God and denial of His signs already supplied more directly above.
It warns when family, wealth, trade, and homes are loved above God and His messenger.
Ibrahim questions his people's devotion to their images, without yet stating their ancestral defense.
Hud calls his people to worship God alone and calls their rival claims fabrication.
It lays out inheritance shares.
Ibrahim declares both the idolaters and their fathers to be in manifest error.
It recounts coercive pressure on Yusuf in the ruler's household.
It contrasts the God who guides to truth with partners that cannot guide themselves.
It names the Day when people hear the true cry and emerge.
It calls the historical outcome a sign while noting that most did not believe.
Pharaoh turns away in power and calls Musa a magician or madman.
It describes the moon following the sun.
Shuayb grounds his reforming call in clear proof from his Lord and refuses to contradict it in practice.
It notes that the Prophet was not among Midian reciting God's verses, yet was sent to relate them.
A powerful people gain no benefit from their faculties because they deny God's signs and mock what warned them.
The people explicitly say Hud came to turn them away from their gods and demand the threatened punishment.
It contrasts hearing the covenant with disobedience and attachment to the calf.
It gives the destruction of Nuh's people after they denied the messengers.
It gives pilgrimage and cooperative-conduct commands, including a prohibition on retaliatory transgression.
It directly pairs fabricating a lie about God with denying truth when it arrives.
When told to follow what God revealed, they instead appeal to the practice of their fathers.
The call to God's revelation is refused through the claim that ancestral practice is sufficient.
Deniers hear the Quran but call it nothing but tales of the ancients.
It condemns inventing a lie about God and falsely claiming revelation, directly exposing false attribution.
People defend an inherited corrupt practice by saying they found their fathers doing it and attribute it to God.
Hud's leading deniers call him foolish and a liar, a related discrediting of a messenger.
Pharaoh's chiefs classify Musa as a learned magician, turning signs into a political threat.
Pharaoh's people precommit to call every sign brought to them magic and refuse belief.
Musa and Harun bring signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, who respond arrogantly.
Pharaoh's people accuse Musa and Harun of coming to turn them from what their fathers practiced.
It condemns those who fabricate lies about God and recalls the curse on wrongdoers.
Earlier peoples tell their messengers that they seek to turn them from their fathers' worship.
When asked what God sent down, deniers answer that it is tales of the ancients.
A change of verse prompts the direct accusation that the messenger is a fabricator.
The wrongdoers dismiss the Prophet as a man under a spell, another messenger-discrediting label.
It challenges humans and jinn to produce the like of the Quran, answering claims of human manufacture.
It rejects invented divinities and demands clear authority for attributing them to God.
Pharaoh accuses Musa of coming with magic to drive them from their land.
The magicians' side calls Musa and Harun two magicians seeking to expel them and overturn their way.
Secret opponents ask whether they will submit to magic while seeing, directly relabeling the message.
They alternate between calling the revelation confused dreams, invented speech, and poetry.
The affluent disbelievers reject a human messenger and deny that God would have sent angels.
They frame obedience to a human like themselves as a loss, extending their status-based dismissal.
Pharaoh's people reject belief in Musa and Harun because they are human and their people are servants.
It asks whether they rejected an unfamiliar message or one not received by their forefathers.
Opponents call the Quran ancient tales written down for the messenger, a human-production charge.
Pharaoh calls Musa's messenger mad, a companion form of discrediting prophetic speech.
Pharaoh's chiefs call Musa a learned magician as they prepare a counter-display.
Ibrahim's people state that they and their fathers worship the idols, supplying the ancestral attachment at issue.
Deniers invoke the fate of themselves and their fathers after death to reject resurrection.
They call the promise made to them and their fathers tales of the ancients.
It asks whether the recited Book is not sufficient, opposing demands that evade the revelation itself.
The command to follow God's revelation is refused in favor of following the path of the fathers.
A community dismisses its human messengers and denies that the Merciful sent anything down.
The community treats its messengers as a bad omen and threatens them, showing active resistance to warning.
Leaders say they never heard this monotheistic call in the ancestral religion and call it an invention.
Nations plan against their messenger and argue with falsehood to refute truth.
Musa is sent with signs and clear authority, yet Pharaoh and his chiefs call him a lying magician.
Pharaoh says Musa will change the people's religion, closely echoing the focus's charge of turning them away.
A believer challenges Pharaoh's plan to kill a man who says God is his Lord and brings clear proofs.
A people reject the messengers who came before and behind them with the command to worship God alone.
Deniers order one another not to listen to this Quran and to drown it out so they may prevail.
They explicitly justify their worship by saying they found their fathers on a way and follow their traces.
Affluent opponents of every prior warner make the same appeal to inherited practice.
They persist in following their fathers even when told the messenger brought better guidance.
When truth came to them, they called it magic and declared disbelief in it.
They turn away from the messenger and call him taught and mad.
They reject resurrection through the appeal that only time destroys them and their fathers.
A son rejects his parents' call to faith and calls the promise given to him and earlier generations ancient tales.
Opponents reduce the messenger to a poet and wait for his downfall.
When they see a sign, they turn away and call it continuing magic.
Nuh's people deny their messenger and call him mad.
Thamud reject following a single human among them and call the message error and madness.
It condemns one who fabricates a lie about God while being called to submission.
Earlier peoples reject clear proofs from their messengers because they are human beings.
When God's verses are recited to him, the denier calls them tales of the ancients.
The opponent calls the Quran nothing but transmitted magic.
He further calls it merely the word of a human, directly denying its revealed source.
